(https://www.acvauctions.com/blog/auto-reconditioning-for-dealerships) Since the NAAA single-defect threshold is $800 (claim B2), a typical whole-vehicle recon bill sits near the level at which a *single* defect would become arbitrable — meaning most real recon spend is made up of individually non-arbitrable items.

**G1. Treat the $800 / 2% threshold as a modeling parameter, not a footnote.** Because each defect must clear it independently (B3) and wearables are excluded (B7), the expected recoverable share of a recon bill is much smaller than the bill. An estimation model that omits the threshold structure will systematically overstate downside protection.

This report covers how a repair (reconditioning) cost figure is produced, used, contested, and evaluated for a vehicle transacted at a wholesale auto auction. In scope: the inputs a cost estimate is built from (condition reports, damage line items, grades, diagnostic scans, battery state-of-health), who is authoritative for the number when money turns on it, the dollar thresholds that make an estimate consequential, and how well automated estimation performs.

This report covers only the estimation of repair and reconditioning cost for a vehicle being bought or sold through an auction channel — wholesale dealer auctions governed by NAAA arbitration rules (Manheim and peers) and salvage/insurance auctions (Copart, IAA). It covers where those estimates break, what they structurally cannot see, and where published sources disagree. It does not cover vehicle valuation, bidding strategy, title branding, transport, or auction selection; those are separate frontier items.

**Claim 1 — The auction condition report is explicitly not a repair cost estimate.** The NAAA Auction Condition Report Position Statement, updated June 1, 2026, states: "ACRs are not intended to diagnose vehicle condition, certify safety or roadworthiness, or estimate repair costs." It adds that "visual inspections are limited in nature and cannot reliably identify mechanical, ADAS, electrical, structural, or battery-related conditions." The condition report is therefore a damage *disclosure* document, not a costing document.

**Claim 2a — The cost basis is wholesale, not retail, and is deliberately narrowed.** The same guidelines limit successful-arbitration reimbursement to "commercially reasonable costs based on local auction (wholesale) repair or transportation rates," and explicitly exclude reconditioning: "Lost profit and commissions along with marketing and reconditioning costs are not reimbursable under any circumstances." Auction repair cost estimation is thus a distinct cost standard from collision-shop or insurance estimating, which price at retail labor rates. Source: https://naaa.com/wp-content/uploads/

**B6. Reconditioning cost is explicitly non-recoverable, so an estimating error is borne entirely by the buyer.** Buyer Responsibilities IV.2: "Following a successful arbitration claim, the buyer will be responsible for, and will not be reimbursed by the seller or auction, any repairs, reconditioning, or enhancements made to the vehicle prior to its return to the auction."
